claim: Developer trust in AI accuracy fell from 40% to 29% in 2025 while favorability dropped from 72% to 60%, and 45% cite 'almost right, but not quite' AI output as their top frustration.
quote: trust in the accuracy of AI has fallen from 40% in previous years to just 29% this year. ... The number-one frustration, cited by 45% of respondents, is dealing with 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.'

claim: Despite 84% of developers using AI tools, more actively distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%), with only 3% saying they highly trust AI output, per the 2025 Stack Overflow survey.
quote: 84% of devs now use AI tools and 51% of pros use them daily, but trust hit an all-time low (46% distrust output, only 3% 'highly trust' it).

claim: The 2025 DORA report finds 30% of developers report little to no trust in AI-generated code, creating a 'verification tax' where time saved in creation is reallocated to auditing AI output.
quote: According to the 2025 DORA report, 30% of developers report little to no trust in AI-generated code. ... While I end up spending less time writing code, I spend more time babysitting the AI and reviewing what it is trying to do.

claim: Most AI code review platforms run 5-15% false positive rates, and teams progress from thorough investigation to 'dismiss all' within roughly 13 weeks as alert fatigue sets in.
quote: Most AI code review platforms operate between 5-15% false positive rates (FPR) ... Week 13+: 'I just click dismiss all now' ... 10% FPR translates to 2.5 wasted engineering hours per week

claim: Automation complacency research shows humans detect only ~30% of errors when AI is reliable versus ~75% when systems fail visibly, and developers with AI assistance wrote less secure code while believing it more secure.
quote: When AI is reliable, humans detect only ~30% of errors vs. ~75% when systems fail visibly (Parasuraman et al., 1993) ... Developers with AI assistance 'wrote significantly less secure code' yet 'were more likely to believe' it was secure (Perry et al., 2023)

claim: A 2025 systematic review of 35 peer-reviewed studies finds automation bias undermines competence by discouraging active reasoning and verification, weakening users' independent judgement and agency.
quote: automation bias—the tendency to over-rely on automated recommendations—has emerged as a critical challenge in human–AI collaboration ... it undermines competence by discouraging active reasoning and verification

claim: Microsoft researchers describe 'AI drag' where AI boosts seniors while undermining how juniors build expertise; a Harvard study of 62M workers found junior developer employment fell 9-10% within six quarters at AI-adopting firms while senior employment was unchanged.
quote: AI is making senior engineers dramatically more productive while simultaneously undermining the mechanisms through which junior engineers develop expertise ... Junior employment dropped 9-10% within six quarters at firms adopting AI ... Senior employment 'remained virtually unchanged'

claim: Code review's primary purpose is knowledge-sharing and education rather than bug-finding, a mentoring function AI tools bypass since they cannot grasp architectural intent or product trade-offs.
quote: treat every review as an opportunity for education and knowledge transfer, reframing code review as a primary mechanism for mentoring ... AI code review tools can surface hundreds of context signals, but they can't always understand architectural intent, product trade-offs

claim: AI coding assistant adoption reached 84% in 2026 while trust sits at only 29%, illustrating a widening adoption-trust gap.
quote: AI Coding Assistant Stats 2026: 84% Adoption, 29% Trust
